title: IT FELT LIKE GOD… BUT WAS IT?
paragraphs:
IT FELT LIKE GOD… BUT WAS IT?
What “Test the Spirits” Really Means Before You Trust That Voice, Follow That Sign, or Call That Feeling God
There is a frightening sentence a Christian can say with absolute sincerity:
“I just feel like God told me.”
Maybe you were sitting alone when an overwhelming thought entered your mind.
Maybe somebody spoke a “prophetic word” over you and somehow knew exactly what you had been struggling with.
Maybe a door suddenly opened after months of prayer.
Maybe you dreamed something so vivid that you woke up trembling.
Maybe you saw the same phrase three times in one day.
Maybe you felt an unusual peace about a relationship.
Maybe a video appeared on your feed at exactly the moment you were asking God for an answer.
But Scripture gives us a warning that can be uncomfortable precisely because it destroys one of our favorite assumptions:
Something can feel spiritual without being from God.
Something can feel powerful without being true.
Something can arrive at the perfect moment and still require testing.
Something can even use Christian language and still deserve examination.
That is why the apostle John did not tell believers to believe everything spiritual.
He told them almost the opposite.
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God...” — 1 John 4:1, KJV
“Ἀγαπητοί, μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα εἰ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστιν...”
Agapētoi, mē panti pneumati pisteuete, alla dokimazete ta pneumata ei ek tou Theou estin...
“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to determine whether they are from God.”
John does not teach spiritual gullibility.
But neither does he teach cynical unbelief.
And notice something beautiful before we go any further.
This warning comes wrapped in love.
God does not teach His children discernment because He wants them frightened of everything spiritual.
He teaches discernment because He loves them too much to leave them vulnerable to deception.
Testing something is not necessarily evidence that your faith is weak.
Sometimes testing it is exactly what biblical faithfulness requires.
You are not dishonoring God by asking whether something truly came from Him.
God Himself commanded His people not to believe every spiritual claim automatically.
And somebody reading this desperately needs that freedom.
Because perhaps you have been afraid to question something.
And because they sounded confident, you became afraid that questioning them meant questioning God.
Or maybe nobody else said anything.
Maybe the voice was inside your own heart.
And that can be even harder.
When you desperately want something to be God's will, almost anything can begin looking like confirmation.
That person you cannot stop thinking about.
That decision you already want to make.
Every open door feels divinely arranged.
And somewhere between desire and interpretation, we can accidentally rename what we want...
That is why biblical discernment matters.
Because your emotions are real, but they are not Scripture.
Your intuition may be useful, but it is not infallible.
Your circumstances matter, but circumstances alone do not define truth.
An open door is not automatically God's door.
A closed door is not automatically God's rejection.
Peace is precious, but subjective peace by itself is not sufficient proof that God has spoken.
A dream can deeply affect you without becoming divine revelation.
A coincidence can make you stop and think without becoming a command from heaven.
And somebody's confidence when saying “God told me” does not give their words the authority of Scripture.
John tells us why caution is necessary:
“...because many false prophets have gone out into the world.”
And John immediately brings the test toward Jesus Christ.
“Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God...” — 1 John 4:2, KJV
The Greek centers the confession on:
Jesus Christ having come in the flesh.

John was confronting false teaching about Christ. His test was not a mystical technique for detecting invisible beings by sensations. The immediate context concerns truth and error expressed through teachers and spiritual claims, especially what they confess concerning Jesus Christ.
In other words, biblical discernment is profoundly Christ-centered.
Does it agree with the Jesus revealed in Scripture?
Does it confess the true Christ rather than reinventing Him?
Does it lead toward obedience to Christ or away from Him?
Does it glorify Christ or subtly enthrone me?
Does it agree with what God has already revealed?
Because God does not need to contradict yesterday's Scripture to give you today's guidance.
The Holy Spirit does not wage war against the Word He inspired.
“Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.” — John 17:17
So if a voice tells you adultery is acceptable because “this person understands me better than my spouse”...
You do not need another sign.
If an impression tells you revenge is justified because somebody deserves to suffer...
You do not need a prophetic confirmation.
If somebody tells you God commanded you to do something Scripture identifies as sin...
You do not need to wonder whether you are resisting the Holy Spirit.
You already have revelation sufficient to reject the claim.
God will never require you to disobey God in order to obey God.
God will never require you to disobey God in order to obey God.
But deception is rarely effective when it arrives looking obviously evil.
That is what makes discernment difficult.
Temptation sometimes arrives looking like relief.
Pride can dress itself as calling.
Selfish ambition can call itself purpose.
Bitterness can disguise itself as discernment.
And sometimes what we call “God closing the door” is simply us refusing to walk through a difficult one.
Sometimes what we call “God giving me peace” is actually the relief we feel after choosing what we wanted all along.
This is why the Christian life cannot safely be built on vibes.
Not every misleading spiritual impression must be blamed directly on a demon.
Our eagerness to interpret ordinary circumstances as extraordinary messages.
“The heart is deceitful above all things...” — Jeremiah 17:9, KJV
That does not mean every emotion is evil.
It means our internal world is not an infallible authority.
Even sincere Christians can sincerely misunderstand something.
Yet when Jesus began explaining that He would suffer and be killed, Peter rebuked Him.
Surely suffering could not be God's plan for the Messiah.
Then Jesus answered Peter with words that should sober every believer who assumes sincerity guarantees discernment:
“Get thee behind me, Satan...” — Matthew 16:23, KJV
Peter was not necessarily consciously trying to serve Satan.
He was thinking wrongly about God's plan.
His feelings about what Jesus should do were colliding with what the Father actually intended.
That means sincerity alone cannot be our test.
Miraculous appearance cannot be our test.
Even supernatural phenomena, by themselves, cannot be the final test.
Jesus warned that false christs and false prophets would show “great signs and wonders” in an attempt to deceive. Paul likewise warned about deception associated with signs and lying wonders.
Scripture therefore never gives us permission to say:
“It was supernatural, therefore it was God.”
Does it agree with God's revealed Word?
Does it confess and honor the biblical Christ?
Does it move you toward holiness, truth, love, humility, repentance and obedience?
Or does it make you increasingly fascinated with yourself?
There is a kind of spirituality where Jesus becomes little more than a supporting character in someone's personal destiny story.
And Jesus quietly disappears behind the enormous shadow of the self.
Because the Holy Spirit's ministry is not to make Christ smaller so we can become enormous.
Not needing another prophetic video every morning before you can make ordinary decisions.
The Spirit of God does not lead us away from Christ into endless fascination with ourselves.
And sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do when something “feels like God” is wait.
You do not have to panic.
You do not have to manufacture certainty.
You do not have to announce it immediately.
You do not have to build your future around one dream tonight.
You do not have to marry someone because somebody prophesied that person was “the one.”
You do not have to quit your job tomorrow because a video appeared on your feed.
You do not have to send money because somebody claims God revealed that your miracle depends upon your offering.
You can seek counsel from mature believers.
You can ask whether your own desires are distorting your judgment.
God is not intimidated by careful biblical discernment.
But there is something deeper here.
Maybe the voice you have struggled most to discern is not somebody else's.
Maybe it is the one inside you saying:
“You've sinned too badly for Jesus to want you.”
“You failed again. God must be finished with you.”
“You should hide from God until you become better.”
Because conviction and condemnation do not produce the same destination.
The Holy Spirit exposes sin, yes.
The cross itself proves how serious sin is.
But the Spirit's conviction drives sinners toward Christ.
Condemnation whispers that you should run away from Him.
The Gospel says something radically different.
But Jesus already knows where you are.
But at Calvary, the sinless Son of God carried the judgment sinners deserved.
But Jesus can redeem what your past means for your future.
And suddenly “test the spirits” becomes more than a warning about false prophets somewhere on the internet.
What voice has been shaping your understanding of God?
The voice of a preacher who made himself indispensable?
Or the truth revealed in Jesus Christ?
Some of us have called anxiety “discernment” for years.
Some have called emotional dependency “God's will.”
And perhaps the most painful question is this:
What if the thing you desperately wanted to be from God...
Because discernment sometimes costs us something.
A decision we wanted God to approve.
An identity we built around a spiritual experience.
But losing an illusion is not losing God.
Sometimes losing the thing falsely labeled “God” is how we rediscover the God who was there all along.
Jesus is not threatened when counterfeit certainty collapses.
When you realize you misunderstood something...
When your emotions scream one thing and Scripture tells you another...
And perhaps this is where grace becomes scandalous.
Because even when you were wrong...
Even when you confused your desire with His voice.
Even when you followed something you should have tested.
Even when you believed somebody who manipulated your hunger for God.
Even when you made the wrong decision.
Even when you said, “God told me,” only to discover later that perhaps He had not...
Grace is not standing at the end of the road laughing at you.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
There is freedom in those words.
“Lord, I wanted it so badly that I called my desire Your voice.”
“Lord, I followed feelings instead of truth.”
“Lord, I trusted someone simply because they sounded spiritual.”
“Lord, I ignored Scripture because I preferred the answer I wanted.”
And the Gospel answers your confession not with a slammed door...
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins...” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice where John ultimately takes his readers after warning them about deception.
Not into fear of demons hiding behind every circumstance.
Not into obsession with detecting invisible enemies.
“Ye are of God, little children, and have overcome them: because greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world.” — 1 John 4:4, KJV
Biblical discernment therefore does not produce terrified Christians suspicious of everything.
It produces believers anchored so deeply in Christ that counterfeits become easier to recognize because they increasingly know the real thing.
Know His character as revealed in Scripture.
Stay close to healthy Christian community.
And when something feels like it came from God...
Does it diminish the biblical Jesus?
Does it make a human teacher functionally unquestionable?
Does it depend primarily on emotional intensity rather than truth?
Does it flatter your pride while avoiding repentance?
Does it make you afraid to test it?
That itself should make you cautious.
But if something agrees with Scripture, magnifies the true Christ, encourages faithful obedience, bears godly fruit, survives wise examination, and remains consistent with the Gospel...
Not arrogantly declaring that every impression you experience carries divine authority.
Because mature discernment does not need theatrics.
And maybe tonight you need to stop asking only:
Maybe you need to stop saying:
“I know it was God because I had peace.”
“Lord, whatever I feel, make me obedient to what You have actually revealed.”
Maybe you need to release something you have been forcing God to endorse.
Maybe you need to admit you were deceived.
Maybe you need to stop hiding.
Or maybe you simply need Jesus again.
Somebody reading silently may need to know that returning to truth is possible.
And if someone you love is making a major decision because something merely “feels like God,” do not use this article as a weapon against them. Send it with love.
Because one day the feeling may become overwhelming.
And on that day you may need to remember three words:

If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, see Jesus more clearly, repent more deeply, or stand stronger in your faith, help us keep that work moving. One practical way to glorify God is to steward what He has given you for the spread of His truth. Salvation and God's grace cannot be bought.
If this truth matters, carry it farther.
Supporting Gospel work can glorify God when it flows from love for Christ rather than pressure, guilt, or an attempt to earn His favor.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A ministry cannot reconcile you to God.
An article cannot transform a dead heart.
So above everything else written here...
And cling to Christ so tightly that when counterfeit voices whisper His name, you recognize that something is wrong because you have learned the voice of truth through His Word.
Maybe the most dangerous spiritual lie is not the one that sounds evil.
Maybe it is the one that sounds almost like God...
while quietly leading you away from Jesus.
And maybe the grace you need tonight is realizing that even if you followed the wrong voice yesterday, Jesus is still calling you back to truth today.
The feeling may have fooled you. The voice may have confused you. The sign may have failed you. But Jesus Christ has not changed—and grace still knows the road home.
